intro: People have played for thousands of years. Greeks ran races at Olympia. People in Mexico built stone courts for a rubber ball. Each kind of play needed its own place.
Today we still build special places. Soccer uses a grass pitch. Basketball began in a gym in 1891. Races use a 400-meter track. Swimmers use pools, and hockey players use rinks.
Games also need turns everyone can see. A whistle, a starting line and a written team size help. You will learn who wrote those rules, and when.
bigQuestion: How do places and written rules help people share a game?

title: Play Has Kinds

chapters.title: Balls, Races, Water, Ice
chapters.bigQuestion: Why do ball games, races, swimming and ice games each need their own place?

story.title: The Floor Changes
story.kicker: A class walks outside and feels the ground change under their shoes.
paragraphs: A second-grade class lines up in the gym. The floor is smooth wood. Two hoops hang high at each end. Every step squeaks a little.
The class walks out the side door. Now the ground is soft grass. White lines mark a long rectangle. A goal net stands at each end.
Past the grass is an oval of red rubber. It has lanes painted in white. A boy taps it with his shoe. It feels springy, not soft.
Back inside, the teacher asks a question. Could you swim on the grass? Could you skate on the wood? Each kind of play needs its own ground.
story.think: What is the ground like in each play place at your school?

lessons.title: Races at Olympia
lessons.mainIdea: Long ago, people in Greece ran races in a stadium at Olympia.
reading: *Olympia* is a place in Greece. Games were held there long ago. The traditional date for the first games is 776 BCE. They came every four years.
A main race was one length of the *stadium*. The stadium was a long, straight dirt track. People sat on grassy banks beside it to watch.

words.d: the place in Greece where the ancient Olympic Games were held
a long place built for races, with room for people to watch

look.title: Two Race Paths
look.text: Look at a long, straight dirt path at old Olympia. Grass banks rise on each side. Now look at a modern red oval with eight white lanes. Both were built so a race has a place.
look.prompt: What is the same about these two paths? What is different?

check.why: The stadium was a long, straight dirt track for races.

check.q: Where did people sit to watch?

lessons.title: Stone Courts for a Rubber Ball
lessons.mainIdea: People in ancient Mexico and Central America built stone courts for a ball game.
reading: People in Mexico and Central America played a ball game long ago. It began more than 3,000 years ago. The ball was made of *rubber* from trees.
Players needed a special place. They built a *ball court* of stone. It was a long, narrow alley. High walls stood on both sides. The largest one is at Chichén Itzá in Mexico.

words.d: a bouncy material made from the sap of certain trees
a long stone alley with walls, built for the ancient Mesoamerican ball game

look.title: The Great Ball Court
look.text: Look at a long grass alley at Chichén Itzá. Tall stone walls rise on each side. High on each wall is a stone ring. People built this court more than 800 years ago.
look.prompt: Why would a ball game need walls instead of an open field?

check.why: The Mesoamerican ball was made of rubber from tree sap.

check.q: What did players build for this game?
check.why: They built long stone ball courts with walls.

check.q: Where is the largest old ball court?
check.why: The largest ancient ball court is at Chichén Itzá in Mexico.

lessons.title: A Pitch for Soccer
lessons.mainIdea: Soccer clubs in London wrote shared rules in 1863, and the game is played on a pitch.
reading: In 1863, clubs in London met at a tavern. They wrote shared rules for a kicking game. They named their group the *Football Association*.
Their game is called soccer in the United States. It is played on a *pitch*. A pitch is a long rectangle of grass or turf. A goal stands at each end.

words.d: the group of English clubs that wrote shared soccer rules in 1863
the grass or turf rectangle where soccer is played

look.title: The Meeting in 1863
look.text: On 26 October 1863, football clubs met at the Freemasons' Tavern in London. They formed the Football Association. They wanted teams from different places to play by the same rules.
look.cite: The Football Association, record of its founding meeting, Freemasons' Tavern, London, 26 October 1863
look.prompt: Why would teams from different places want the same rules?

lessons.title: A Game Made for a Gym
lessons.mainIdea: James Naismith made basketball for a gym in Springfield, Massachusetts, in 1891.
reading: *James Naismith* taught at a school in Springfield, Massachusetts. In December 1891, winter kept his class inside. The students were bored and restless.
Naismith needed a game that fit a *gym*. He nailed two peach baskets to the balcony. Players tossed a soccer ball at them. That game became basketball.

words.d: the teacher who made up basketball in 1891
a big indoor room with a hard floor, built for games and exercise

look.title: Naismith's Winter Class
look.text: Naismith wrote that his class at the YMCA training school needed an indoor game for the winter of 1891. He used a soccer ball and two peach baskets.
look.cite: James Naismith, Basketball: Its Origin and Development (1941)
look.prompt: Why did the season matter to where the game was played?

check.q: In what town did basketball begin?
check.why: Naismith taught in Springfield, Massachusetts.

lessons.title: A Lap of 400 Meters
lessons.mainIdea: One lap in the inside lane of a standard outdoor track is 400 meters.
reading: A modern running *track* is an oval. It has painted *lanes*. Each runner stays in one lane. Lanes keep runners from bumping.
One lap in the inside lane is 400 meters. World Athletics sets that size. Tracks around the world match it. So a time in one town can be compared with another.

words.d: an oval path with lanes, built for running races
a marked strip that one runner stays in during a race

lessons.title: A Pool Has Walls
lessons.mainIdea: Swim races need a pool with a measured length from wall to wall.
reading: Swimmers race in a *pool*. A pool is a tank of water with walls. Its length is measured. Swimmers touch the wall at each end.
Many school pools in the United States are 25 yards long. The Olympic Games use a longer pool. It is 50 meters from wall to wall.

words.d: a tank of water with walls, measured for swim races

look.title: Two Pools
look.text: Look at a school pool. It is 25 yards long. A swimmer touches the far wall quickly. Now look at an Olympic pool. It is 50 meters long. The far wall looks much farther away.
look.prompt: Which pool would take longer to swim across? How do you know?

check.q: How long is an Olympic pool?
check.why: The Olympic Games use a pool 50 meters long.

check.q: What do swimmers touch at each end?
check.why: A pool has walls, and swimmers touch the wall at each end.

lessons.title: Ice Needs a Rink
lessons.mainIdea: Ice hockey moved indoors to a rink, and an NHL rink is 200 feet long.
reading: Hockey is played on ice. People once played on frozen ponds. In 1875, a game was played indoors in Montreal, Canada. It was at the Victoria Skating *Rink*.
A rink is a floor of ice with walls around it. Today a *National Hockey League* rink is 200 feet long. It is 85 feet wide. The corners are curved.

words.d: a floor of ice with walls around it, used for hockey and skating
the top professional hockey league in the United States and Canada, called the NHL

chapters.title: A Turn Everyone Can See
chapters.bigQuestion: How do a whistle, a line and a written number help everyone take fair turns?

story.title: Half Freeze, Half Run
story.kicker: One sharp sound tells a whole field what to do.
paragraphs: It is field day. Sixteen children stand on the grass. Eight stand with their toes behind a white line. Eight wait on the side.
The teacher lifts a whistle. Tweet! The eight at the line dash forward. The eight on the side stay still. They know their turn comes next.
Nobody had to shout. Nobody had to argue. The line showed where to wait. The whistle showed when to go. Everyone could see and hear the same thing.
Grown-up sports use the same tools. A referee holds a whistle. A track has a starting line. A rule book says how many may play.
story.think: What tells you when it is your turn at school?

lessons.title: The Referee's Whistle
lessons.mainIdea: In soccer, the referee is the one person who starts and stops play.
reading: A soccer match has a *referee*. The rule book for soccer is the Laws of the Game. Law 5 says the referee starts and stops play.
The referee uses a *whistle*. Its sharp sound carries across a big field. Every player hears the same signal at once. Fans hear it too.

words.d: the official who is in charge of a soccer match
a small tool that makes a sharp sound to start or stop play

look.title: Law 5: The Referee
look.text: Each match is controlled by a referee. The referee has full authority to enforce the Laws of the Game. The referee can stop, pause or end a match.
look.cite: IFAB, Laws of the Game, Law 5 (The Referee)
look.prompt: Why is it helpful that only one person holds this power?

check.q: Who starts and stops a soccer match?
check.why: Law 5 of the Laws of the Game gives this job to the referee.

check.q: Why does a whistle help on a big field?
check.why: The whistle's sharp sound carries across a big field.

check.q: What is soccer's rule book called?
check.why: Soccer's rule book is the Laws of the Game.

lessons.title: Wait Behind the Line
lessons.mainIdea: Runners wait behind one starting line so every racer begins from the same place.
reading: A race begins at a starting *line*. Every runner waits behind it. That way no one starts closer to the finish.
Runners must wait for the start signal. Leaving too soon is a *false start*. Under World Athletics rules, a false start can remove a runner from the race.

words.d: a painted mark that shows where a race begins
leaving before the start signal

look.title: Toes Behind the Paint

look.prompt: Why did the starter call everyone back?

check.why: A false start is leaving before the signal.

check.q: Whose rules say a false start can remove a runner?

lessons.title: Eleven on a Soccer Side
lessons.mainIdea: The Laws of the Game let each soccer team have eleven players on the pitch.
reading: Law 3 of the Laws of the Game is about players. It says a team has up to eleven players on the pitch. One of the eleven is the *goalkeeper*.
Other players wait at the side. They are *substitutes*. A substitute may come on when the referee allows it. Then a player on the pitch comes off.

words.d: the player who guards a team's goal
players who wait at the side and may come on later

look.prompt: How many more players does a soccer team have than a basketball team?

check.why: Law 3 allows up to eleven players per team.

check.q: Who is one of the eleven?
check.why: The goalkeeper is one of the eleven players.

check.q: When may a substitute come on?
check.why: A substitute comes on when the referee allows it.

lessons.title: From Nine to Five
lessons.mainIdea: Basketball began with nine players a side, and later rules set five.
reading: Naismith's first class had eighteen students. So his first game used nine players on each *team*. That was in December 1891.
Nine players crowded the small gym. Within a few years, rule makers chose five a side. Today five players per team are on the *court*.

words.d: a group of players who play on the same side
the marked floor where basketball is played

look.title: The First Class
look.text: Naismith wrote that his class had eighteen men. He picked two captains. The captains chose sides, nine on each team, and the first game began.
look.cite: James Naismith, Basketball: Its Origin and Development (1941)
look.prompt: Why did the first game have nine on a side?

check.q: How many students were in Naismith's first class?
check.why: Eighteen students made two teams of nine.

check.q: How many basketball players per team are on the court today?
check.why: Today the rules put five players per team on the court.

check.q: Why did rule makers change from nine?
check.why: Nine a side crowded the gym, so later rules set five.

lessons.title: Naismith Posts His Rules
lessons.mainIdea: Naismith wrote thirteen rules and posted them so every player could read them.
reading: Before the first game, Naismith wrote his *rules*. There were thirteen. He pinned them on a board in the gym. Every player could read them.
In January 1892, the rules were printed. They appeared in the school paper, The Triangle. Soon other schools could play the same game.

words.d: written words that say what players may and may not do

look.title: A Paper on the Board
look.text: Look at a sheet of paper pinned to a gym wall. It is 1891. Thirteen short rules are written on it. Eighteen students crowd around to read it before they play.
look.prompt: Why did Naismith pin the rules where everyone could see them?

check.why: Naismith wrote thirteen rules for the first game.

check.q: Where were the rules printed in 1892?

lessons.title: Fair Means the Same Rule
lessons.mainIdea: A game is fair when both sides use the same written rules.
reading: A *fair* game uses one set of rules for both sides. Both soccer teams follow the same Laws of the Game. Both have eleven players.
In 1886, four British football groups formed the *IFAB*. It still guards the Laws of the Game. So a match in Brazil uses the same laws as one in Chicago.

words.d: using the same rules for each side
the International Football Association Board, formed in 1886, which keeps the Laws of the Game

look.title: Two Teams, One Book
look.text: Look at two teams walking onto a pitch. One team is from Brazil. One is from Chicago. They speak different languages. They follow the same seventeen Laws of the Game.
look.prompt: How can two teams play together if they speak different languages?

check.q: When was the IFAB formed?

check.q: What does the IFAB keep?

lessons.mainIdea: The Illinois High School Association, begun in 1900, runs state contests for Illinois schools.
reading: In 1900, Illinois schools formed the *Illinois High School Association*. People call it the IHSA. It helps schools across the state follow shared rules.
The IHSA runs state contests. The first boys wrestling state champions were crowned in 1937. Girls wrestling had its first state finals in 2022.

words.d: the group that runs state school sports in Illinois, begun in 1900; also called the IHSA
